sections.heading: Welcome Video
paragraphs: In this short welcome video I introduce myself, walk you through how this course works, and frame what you’re signing up for. I cover the “pain before magic” teaching philosophy, where sometimes you solve a problem with clunky tools so that the right tool, when it arrives, actually sticks. I also lay out the five-module arc that takes you from variables and decisions through loops, functions, files, and dictionaries, all the way to classes and objects (Python chapters 2 through 10).

You’ll learn that in this course you aren’t a student, you’re a Junior Developer at Bat City Collective, an Austin indie game studio building a retro Texas road trip game called Deep in the Heart: A Lone Star Journey for our client, All My Eggses Live in Texas. I introduce the five mentor voices you’ll hear all semester (Danny, Priya, Sasha, T-Bone, and Tyler), and explain the BUILD → ENHANCE → MASTER rhythm where each module’s three labs build on the same growing codebase.

I also walk through the logistics: every lab is auto-graded by CodeGrade with the same five-category rubric for everyone, Discord is the first stop for questions and email is for anything personal or FERPA-sensitive, our weekly Tuesday 6 PM Central Zoom is open Q&A for both my classes, and there’s no late work but the lowest grade in each category drops automatically. AI is allowed for explanations and debugging, not for generating code you submit, and you should be ready to defend any line you turn in.

The video closes with your first 72 hours: install Python and VS Code, read the syllabus and the Lab 1.1 assignment sheet, join Discord using the invite link on the Discord page in the left navigation, and get your first BookEx and Lab 1.1 submitted by the end of the first week.

sections.html: Welcome to IS2053! Before diving into Python, let’s make sure you’re fully set up for success. Complete each checkpoint below in order. They are designed to build on each other. Most students finish in 80–110 minutes.

sections.name: Danny Cavanaugh
sections.quote: “Hey there! I’m Danny, and I’ll be your guide through this course. Don’t rush through these setup steps. A solid foundation saves hours of frustration later. If you hit any snags, swing by Tuesday office hours on Zoom. We’re here to help!”

sections.title: A note on AI, before you read anything else
sections.body_html: I used AI to help write parts of this site, including a lot of the CSS behind the layout and much of the wording on the lab pages. The AI Policy page says exactly where and why. I ask you to be honest about your use of it, so I am being honest about mine.

preContent.html: Twelve checkpoints. Plan on 80–110 minutes total. Each checkpoint shows its time estimate so you can split this across multiple sittings if you need to.

preContent.title: Don’t Rush the Installs
preContent.body_html: Checkpoints 3–9 set up your entire development environment. If something goes wrong here, every future assignment gets harder. Take your time and verify each step works before moving on.

body.html: The syllabus contains essential information about grading, policies, and course structure. Find it in the Syllabus link in the left navigation. Pay special attention to the grading breakdown and late work policy.

checkpoints.title: Read “The Scenario”
checkpoints.subBanner: 10 minutes: Meet the team and the client

body.html: Meet Bat City Collective, your mentors, the client (All My Eggses Live in Texas), and learn about the game you’ll be building all semester. This sets up the story and gives context to every lab assignment!

Download Python from python.org. Get version 3.14 or newer. One heads-up before you click anything: python.org now pushes you toward its new Install Manager as the front-and-center download button. For this course, scroll past the Install Manager and grab the standalone installer instead. The first callout below shows you exactly where to look.

body.title: Windows: Skip the Big Install Manager Button
body.body_html:
Mac users: ignore this callout. Click the regular macOS download button and you’re good.

Windows users: the download page recently changed. The most prominent button now reads “Download Python install manager”. That is NOT what we want for this course.

Look just below that big button for a smaller line that reads:
“Or get the standalone installer for Python 3.XX.X”

Click that link. Your download starts automatically and the file will be named something like python-3.14.x-amd64.exe.

body.title: Look for “Add Python to PATH”
body.body_html:
If the installer shows an “Add Python to PATH” checkbox on the first screen, check it before clicking Install.

Not seeing the checkbox? No problem. Some installer versions skip it, especially if you previously had Python installed on this machine. PATH usually gets handled automatically in that case. We’ll verify everything works end-to-end when you run your first program in BookEx 0, and that assignment sheet has a fix-it guide if PATH turns out to be the issue.

body.html: Download Visual Studio Code from code.visualstudio.com. This is our code editor for the semester. It is free, powerful, and used by professional developers worldwide.

checkpoints.title: Disable AI Autocomplete in VS Code

body.html: VS Code now ships with AI-powered code suggestions turned on by default. It sounds helpful, but it will hurt you in this course. The AI doesn’t know what chapter we’re on, so it happily suggests list comprehensions, f-strings, and other techniques we haven’t covered yet. CodeGrade flags those as scope violations and auto-zeroes the assignment. The suggestions are also frequently just wrong for your specific problem.

You’ll work in two different panels in VS Code for this checkpoint: first Settings, then Extensions. The keyboard shortcuts and search bars are different in each, so the steps below tell you which panel to switch to before each search.
Open Settings with Cmd + , (Mac) or Ctrl + , (Windows). Use the search bar at the top of the Settings page:

items: Search editor.inlineSuggest.enabled and uncheck the box. This kills the gray ghost-text predictions that appear inline as you type.

body.html: Now switch to Extensions with Cmd + Shift + X (Mac) or Ctrl + Shift + X (Windows). The search bar at the top of the Extensions sidebar is a different search bar from the one in Settings. It searches installed and available extensions, not settings keys.

items: Search GitHub Copilot. If you see it in your installed list, click the gear icon and choose Uninstall. (If it’s not installed, skip this one. Nothing to do.)

Search GitHub Copilot Chat. This is the tricky one. New VS Code installs ship Copilot Chat as a built-in extension, which means there’s no Uninstall button, only a dropdown labeled “Disable AI Features”. Click the dropdown and choose Disable AI Features. This is the step that turns off the right-side CHAT panel and the “Generate code” inline prompt. Both of those come from Copilot Chat, not from the inline suggestion setting in Step 1.
Search IntelliCode. Disable (or uninstall) both IntelliCode and IntelliCode API Usage Examples using the gear icon on each.

body.title: How to Verify It Worked
body.body_html:
After making all the changes above, you should see no AI surfaces anywhere in VS Code. Specifically, all three of these things should be gone:

  • No gray ghost-text appearing inline as you type. Basic autocomplete is fine and expected. Python keywords like if, while, print and variable names you’ve already typed will still pop up in a suggestion dropdown. What should be gone is entire lines of suggested code appearing in gray ahead of your cursor. If those are still there, the editor.inlineSuggest.enabled setting did not take. Go back and re-check Step 1.
  • No “Generate code” inline prompt floating in the editor near your cursor. That prompt comes from Copilot Chat, not from the inline suggestion setting. If you still see it, Copilot Chat’s AI features are still enabled.
  • No CHAT panel on the right side of the VS Code window. Same source: the right-side CHAT panel disappears once Copilot Chat’s AI features are disabled.

If any of these are still showing up, go back to the Extensions panel and confirm GitHub Copilot Chat reads “AI Features Disabled” next to its name.

body.html: I can’t enforce this from my end. But students who lean on AI suggestions in the early modules consistently struggle harder later, because they never built the foundation. See the full AI Policy for the longer version of why.

checkpoints.title: Install the Python Extension
checkpoints.subBanner: 2 minutes: Syntax highlighting and run button

body.html: In VS Code, click the Extensions icon (or press Ctrl+Shift+X). Search for “Python” and install the one by Microsoft. This gives you syntax highlighting, error detection, and the run button.
Still in Extensions, search for “Flake8” and install the one by Microsoft. Flake8 checks your code style: things like consistent spacing, proper indentation, and unused variables.

body.title: This Is Graded
body.body_html: CodeGrade uses Flake8 to check your code style on every submission. Installing it now means you’ll see the same warnings before you submit, so you can fix them and earn full points.

body.title: How It Works
body.body_html: After installing, you’ll see yellow/red squiggly lines under style issues in your code. Hover over them to see what’s wrong and how to fix it. We have a full Flake8 Guide in Canvas that explains every error code.

checkpoints.title: Set Up Your Workspace Folder
checkpoints.subBanner: 5 minutes: The folder structure that keeps you sane

body.html: You’re going to write a lot of code this semester. One folder per assignment is the simplest way to keep work organized, recover when something breaks, and avoid accidentally overwriting your previous lab.

Keeping a code base organized is a real skill. It is one of the unglamorous habits that separates developers who ship clean work from ones who lose half a day every week to “where did I put that?” Never organized a code base before? Don’t worry about it. I’ve set up the folder structure for you in the starter zip below, along with empty .py file templates pre-named exactly what CodeGrade expects. Just download it, drop it in your Documents folder, open the assignment folder when it’s time to work, and fill in the file. The organization is handled.
Download and unzip the starter folder:

body.title: Extract the Zip First. Do Not Work Inside It.
body.body_html:
Double-clicking a .zip does not unpack it. Windows opens a preview window and quietly copies the contents into a temporary folder, and VS Code then runs your file from there. Windows deletes that folder whenever it feels like it, so code you write and save can simply vanish.

The tell: a path with the name doubled in it, like ...\Temp\is2053-starter.zip.is2053-starter.zip\is2053\.... If you see that, you are working inside the zip.

Do this instead: find is2053-starter.zip in your Downloads folder, right-click it, choose Extract All, and extract to somewhere permanent such as Documents. Not Downloads, not Desktop, not Temp. Then open that extracted is2053 folder in VS Code with File → Open Folder. That folder is your home base for the semester.

body.html: Unzip it into your Documents folder, or anywhere easy to find. One small note: cloud-synced folders (OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive) can occasionally cause file-locking issues when VS Code, Python, and the cloud syncer all try to touch the same file at once. Most students never see this. I sync my own course code through OneDrive without issue. If you ever get a mysterious “file is locked” or “permission denied” error mid-edit, cloud sync is the first thing to check.
You’ll end up with this folder tree:

body.title: Each Folder Is Pre-Configured for Python
body.body_html:
Every assignment folder in the zip ships with a hidden .vscode/ sub-folder containing workspace settings tuned for this course. When you open one of these folders in VS Code, you’ll automatically see:

  • Three faint vertical lines in the editor, at columns 4, 8, and 79. The first two are visual guides for your first and second indent levels. The third is the PEP 8 line-length limit, and Flake8 will flag any line that crosses it.
  • Tab key inserts 4 spaces, not a tab character. Python style requires spaces, and CodeGrade will reject mixed indentation.
  • Files save with LF line endings, not Windows-style CRLF. CodeGrade runs on Linux and expects LF. Using the zip means you never have to think about this.
  • The Play button always runs your file, instead of dumping you into a >>> prompt. (Newer versions of the Python extension have a bug where the Play button opens an interactive shell instead of executing the script. The starter workspace disables the setting that causes this.)

You don’t need to do anything to enable any of this. It just works once you open the folder. If you’re curious, peek inside any .vscode/settings.json to see what’s configured.

body.title: Building your own folder? Click for line endings note
body.body_html:
If you opted out of the starter zip and built your own folder structure, you’ll want to know about line endings, one of the silent ways CodeGrade can reject code that runs fine on your machine.

The problem: Windows saves files with CRLF line endings (carriage return + line feed). CodeGrade runs on Linux, which expects LF only. That extra carriage return character can garble your output to the autograder even though it looks fine in VS Code.

The symptom: Your code prints the expected output locally, but CodeGrade says the output is wrong, especially when the expected output spans multiple lines and the autograder reports it as one mashed-up line.

The 5-second fix:

  1. Open your .py file in VS Code
  2. Look at the bottom-right corner of the window. You will see CRLF
  3. Click on CRLF
  4. Select LF from the dropdown
  5. Save the file
  6. Resubmit to CodeGrade

The permanent fix: Open VS Code Settings (Cmd + , on Mac, Ctrl + , on Windows), search for eol, and change Files: Eol to \n (LF). Every new file you create will use LF from now on. (This is exactly what the starter zip’s .vscode/settings.json does. If you used the zip, you already have this and can ignore this entire section.)

If your code runs correctly on your machine but CodeGrade gives you weird output errors, check your line endings before you panic.

body.title: Building your own folder? Click for Play-button-shows->>> note
body.body_html:
Recent versions of VS Code’s Python extension have a bug where clicking the Play button on a .py file opens an interactive Python shell (a >>> prompt) instead of running your script. Frustrating because it looks like the Play button is doing nothing useful.

The fix: In VS Code Settings (Cmd + , on Mac, Ctrl + , on Windows), search for REPL Smart Send, and uncheck Python › REPL: Enable REPL Smart Send. Restart VS Code. The Play button will now run your file like normal.

If you used the starter zip, the workspace already disables this setting and you’ll never see the bug.

body.title: The One Rule That Makes Everything Easier
body.body_html:
Always “File → Open Folder” on the specific assignment folder you’re working in. Never the parent is2053/ or code/ folder.

Why? When you open the assignment folder directly, Python automatically looks in that folder for data files like hazards.txt or city_info.txt. Open the parent folder instead, and Python looks in the parent. The data files are nowhere to be found and you get FileNotFoundError errors that make no sense.

Example for Lab 4.3: open is2053/code/modules/mod4/lab-4-3/ as the workspace, not is2053/. Drag the assignment folder onto the VS Code icon, or use File → Open Folder and pick it.

body.title: Why So Many Folders?
body.body_html: Modules 1–3 keep things simple: each lab is a single .py file in its own folder. Once you hit Module 4, your labs add a function_library.py module plus data files (city_distances.txt, hazards.txt, trivia.txt, etc.). Module 5 introduces multi-file class projects. Per-assignment folders isolate each lab’s data and prevent old files from leaking into new work.

checkpoints.title: Submit BookEx 0: Your Setup Check
checkpoints.subBanner: 20–30 minutes: Prove the whole toolchain works and bank your first 100 points

body.html: Everything is installed. Now you prove it works, and you get graded for it. BookEx 0 - Setup Check is a 100-point assignment with two short programs. hello.py comes with the code provided in full, and it confirms that VS Code, Python, and CodeGrade are connected end to end. variable_demo.py is typed straight from your textbook, and it confirms your book is in your hands before Chapter 2 work starts depending on it.

Open it from Canvas, not from a link on this page. Go to Modules. Module 0 • CodeGrade Hello World is the first module on the page, and BookEx 0 - Setup Check is the only thing in it. That is where the full walkthrough lives and where the CodeGrade submission window opens, so working from Canvas keeps both in one place. The walkthrough covers opening the folder, writing the code, running it, first-time CodeGrade signup, and what to do if the Play button fights you.

body.title: Graded, and Due Wednesday
body.body_html:
BookEx 0 is worth 100 points and is due Wednesday, August 26 at 11:59 PM Central.

This is also the first time you will submit to CodeGrade, which means creating your account and paying for semester access. Budget a few extra minutes for that, and do not leave it for Wednesday night.

body.html: Our Discord server is where you can ask questions, get help from classmates, and share wins. Find the join link on the Discord page in the left navigation. Participation is optional but highly recommended!
Post in the Discord: Introductions forum. Tell us your name, major, and one thing you hope to build with Python someday.
You’re ready! Head to Module 1 and open Lab 1.1: Welcome to San Antonio. This is where you’ll write your first real Python program for the game.
Remember: Build a little, test it, fix it. Don’t try to write everything at once!
